content: Histamine is an organic nitrogen compound that plays a critical role in local immune responses, regulates physiological functions in the gastrointestinal tract, and acts as a neurotransmitter in the nervous system. It is a key mediator of the inflammatory response. During immune responses to foreign pathogens, histamine is synthesized and released by basophils and mast cells, which are located in connective tissues near the site of infection or injury. Histamine increases the permeability of capillaries, allowing white blood cells and proteins to access and combat foreign invaders in affected tissues. It is present in nearly all animal body cells. Histamine forms colorless, hygroscopic crystals that melt at 84°C. It dissolves readily in water and ethanol but is insoluble in ether. In aqueous solutions, histamine exists in two tautomeric forms: Nπ-H-histamine and Nτ-H-histamine. It has two basic centers: the aliphatic amino group and the nitrogen atom in the imidazole ring that is not protonated. Typically, histamine is protonated to form a singly charged cation. Histamine is synthesized through the decarboxylation of the amino acid histidine, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme L-histidine decarboxylase. It is a hydrophilic, vasoactive amine. Once formed, histamine is either stored or rapidly inactivated by its primary degradative enzymes, histamine-N-methyltransferase or diamine oxidase. In the central nervous system, histamine released into synapses is primarily broken down by histamine-N-methyltransferase, while in other tissues, both enzymes may contribute to its degradation. Additional enzymes, such as monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) and aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), further process histamine metabolites for excretion or recycling. Certain bacteria can also produce histamine using histidine decarboxylase enzymes distinct from those in animals. A non-infectious foodborne illness, scombroid poisoning, results from bacterial histamine production in spoiled foods, particularly fish. Fermented foods and beverages naturally contain small amounts of histamine due to similar bacterial or yeast activity. For example, sake contains histamine in the range of 20–40 mg/L, while wines contain 2–10 mg/L. In the body, most histamine is stored in granules within mast cells or basophils, which are types of white blood cells. Mast cells are abundant in areas prone to injury, such as the nose, mouth, feet, internal body surfaces, and blood vessels. Non-mast cell histamine is found in various tissues, including the brain, where it functions as a neurotransmitter. Another significant site of histamine storage and release is the enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the stomach. The primary mechanism of histamine release from mast cells and basophils is immunologic. These cells, when sensitized by IgE antibodies bound to their membranes, degranulate upon exposure to the appropriate antigen. Certain drugs, such as morphine and curare alkaloids, can displace histamine from granules and trigger its release. Antibiotics like polymyxin are also known to stimulate histamine release. Histamine exerts its effects by binding to specific cellular histamine receptors. Four histamine receptors have been identified, designated H1 through H4, all of which are G protein-coupled receptors. In the nasal mucosa, histamine increases vascular permeability, causing fluid to escape from capillaries into tissues. This leads to classic allergic symptoms such as a runny nose and watery eyes. Allergens can bind to IgE-loaded mast cells in the nasal mucosa, triggering three clinical responses: sneezing due to histamine-induced sensory neural stimulation, hypersecretion from glandular tissue, and nasal mucosal congestion caused by vascular engorgement associated with vasodilation and increased capillary permeability. Histamine also plays a role in sleep regulation. It is released as a neurotransmitter by neurons located in the posterior hypothalamus, specifically in the tuberomammillary nuclei. These histaminergic neurons project throughout the brain, including to the cortex via the medial forebrain bundle. Histaminergic activity modulates sleep-wake cycles. Antihistamines, which are H1 histamine receptor antagonists, induce sleep. Similarly, destruction of histamine-releasing neurons or inhibition of histamine synthesis results in an inability to maintain wakefulness. Conversely, H3 receptor antagonists promote wakefulness. Histaminergic neurons exhibit the most wakefulness-related firing patterns of any neuronal type recorded to date. They fire rapidly during wakefulness, slow down during relaxation or tiredness, and cease firing entirely during REM and non-REM sleep. These neurons can begin firing just before an animal shows signs of waking. While histamine has stimulatory effects on neurons, it also has suppressive effects that protect against convulsions, drug sensitization, denervation supersensitivity, ischemic lesions, and stress. It has been suggested that histamine regulates mechanisms involved in memory and learning, particularly in the forgetting process. Histamine also influences sexual function. Loss of libido and erectile dysfunction can occur with the use of H2 receptor antagonists, such as cimetidine and ranitidine. Injection of histamine into the corpus cavernosum of men with psychogenic impotence induces full or partial erections in 74% of cases. It has been proposed that H2 antagonists may cause sexual dysfunction by reducing testosterone uptake. In schizophrenia, histamine metabolites are elevated in the cerebrospinal fluid, while the efficiency of H1 receptor binding sites is reduced. Many atypical antipsychotic medications increase histamine turnover. As a key component of the immune system, histamine is implicated in immune system disorders and allergies. In medical literature, histamine is occasionally referred to as H substance or substance H, particularly in the context of allergic skin reactions and tissue responses to inflammation.
